The paper investigates the use of polarization effects in electromagnetic inverse scattering problems.
Polarization provides additional information about the scatterer's properties, such as size, composition, and surface characteristics.
The study focuses on elastic objects like spheres and tori, as well as bubbles in liquids.
The acoustic glory is a phenomenon where certain waves transmitted through a sphere produce a strong backscattered signal.
Diffraction theory is used to correct the unphysical infinities predicted by elementary geometrical acoustics.
The experiments used a digital signal averager and a digital tone burst generator to measure backscattering from elastic spheres.
Rayleigh waves, which are surface waves, significantly contribute to the backscattering from elastic spheres when ka < 100.
The angular dependence of Rayleigh wave scattering is modeled using a Bessel function.
The mixed-mode acoustical glory involves at least one mode conversion (L-to-S or S-to-L) due to internal reflection.
The focal parameters of the mixed-mode acoustical glory are independent of the mode sequence, but the contributions depend on the sequence.
The paper observes strong cross-polarization in the near-forward and backward scattering from bubbles.
The radiation torque on a sphere caused by a circularly polarized electromagnetic wave is investigated.
The research has implications for sonar calibration and optical measurement techniques.
The digital signal averager and digital tone burst generator were used to acquire and analyze the data.
The theoretical models are validated through experimental measurements, with some cases showing agreement better than 1%.
The findings have practical applications in sonar calibration, optical measurement of bubble properties, and the development of novel retro-reflectors for use in water.
